blocks.text: You may be asked to perform any of the following tasks:
Explain hysterosalpingography (HSG) to a woman undergoing infertility investigations.
Counsel a patient about hysterosalpingo-contrast sonography (HyCoSy).
Interpret HSG images showing patent or blocked fallopian tubes.
Discuss the investigations used to assess tubal patency.
Explain the management of bilateral tubal obstruction.
Discuss the complications, contraindications and preparation for tubal patency testing.
Key objective: Demonstrate that you understand why tubal patency matters, how each test is performed, how to interpret the results and how the findings affect fertility management.
The fallopian tubes transport the ovum from the ovary toward the uterus and are the usual site of fertilisation.
For natural conception to occur, at least one tube should generally be functionally patent, with sufficient tubal mobility and mucosal function.
Tubal damage may result from:
Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), including previous chlamydial or gonococcal infection.
Previous ectopic pregnancy.
Endometriosis and pelvic adhesions.
Previous pelvic or abdominal surgery.
Genital tuberculosis, particularly relevant in some settings.
Congenital tubal abnormalities or previous tubal sterilisation.
Important distinction: A tube that appears open on imaging may still have impaired function. Tubal patency does not guarantee normal ovum pickup, ciliary function or transport.
If the station asks you to counsel a patient, begin with a patient-centred approach.

“Good morning. My name is … I understand that you are undergoing investigations to help us understand why you have not conceived. One of the things we may need to check is whether your fallopian tubes are open.

“There are a few ways to do this. I will explain the available options, how the test is performed, the possible discomforts and risks, and what the results could mean for your fertility treatment. Please stop me at any point if you have questions.”
Then:
Confirm the patient's identity.
Establish what she already understands about the investigation.
Ask about concerns, pain, previous experiences and preferences.
Explain the procedure, benefits, alternatives and risks.
Obtain informed consent before proceeding.
Offer a chaperone for intimate procedures and preserve privacy.

subsections.subsection_title: Main methods of assessing tubal patency

blocks.text: Contrast is introduced through the cervix while fluoroscopic images show the uterine cavity, tubes and any spill of contrast into the peritoneal cavity.

items: Ultrasound with contrast or echogenic fluid

blocks.text: A contrast agent or suitable fluid is introduced through the cervix, and ultrasound is used to assess its passage through the tubes.
Dye is introduced through the cervix while a laparoscope is used to observe whether it exits the fimbrial ends of the tubes. It can also identify pelvic adhesions and endometriosis.

rows: Selected cases with suspected pelvic pathology

blocks.text: Choice depends on local expertise, availability, clinical history and patient preference.
Ask about:
Last menstrual period and possibility of pregnancy.
Menstrual cycle regularity.
Previous PID, sexually transmitted infections or pelvic infection.
Previous ectopic pregnancy.
Previous pelvic or tubal surgery.
Previous reactions to contrast media, especially iodinated contrast if HSG uses it.
Allergies and relevant medical conditions.
Current pelvic pain, fever or abnormal vaginal discharge.
Current medication and any relevant bleeding concerns.
HSG is generally performed after menstrual bleeding has ended and before ovulation, commonly during the early follicular phase.

The exact timing depends on cycle length and local protocol. Pregnancy must be excluded. If cycles are irregular or pregnancy cannot be confidently excluded, further assessment or rescheduling may be needed.

content_groups.group_title: C. Contraindications and reasons to defer

blocks.text: Do not proceed without appropriate assessment when there is:
Known or possible pregnancy.
Active pelvic infection or cervicitis.
Significant unexplained pelvic pain or fever suggesting infection.
A relevant severe contrast-agent reaction requiring specialist review or an alternative test.
Recent uterine procedures and other clinical circumstances may require individual assessment.
OSCE pearl: Do not assume that giving prophylactic antibiotics makes HSG safe during active pelvic infection. Active infection should be assessed and treated before the procedure.
Confirm identity, indication and consent. Review pregnancy status, infection risk and contrast history.
Position the patient. Place her supine in the lithotomy position and maintain privacy with an appropriate chaperone.
Perform a speculum examination. Visualise the cervix and clean it using the local sterile technique.
Introduce the cannula or catheter. Position it through the cervix using the selected technique.
Instil contrast gradually. Under fluoroscopic guidance, observe the uterine cavity, filling of both fallopian tubes and any peritoneal spill.
Obtain the required images. The radiologist evaluates uterine contour, tubal course, filling defects, obstruction and spill.
Remove the catheter and allow recovery. Assess discomfort, bleeding, vasovagal symptoms and any immediate adverse reaction.
Explain follow-up. Discuss when and how the result will be communicated and what additional assessment might be required.
The exact catheter, contrast and imaging technique vary by institution. HSG is normally performed by trained personnel in an appropriate imaging facility.
Explain that she may experience:
Menstrual-like cramping during contrast instillation.
Mild spotting afterward.
Temporary discomfort or a brief vasovagal episode.
Less commonly, infection, contrast reaction or other complications.
Analgesia may be offered according to local protocol and the patient's medical history.
Normal-appearing uterine cavity.
Contrast fills both fallopian tubes.
Free bilateral peritoneal spill is seen.
Interpretation: Both tubes appear patent.
One tube fills and spills contrast.
The other tube fails to fill fully or fails to demonstrate spill.
Interpretation: Possible unilateral obstruction; assess for spasm, technical difficulty and the location of the suspected block.

items: Both tubes fail to fill beyond the uterine cornua.

blocks.text: Interpretation: Possible bilateral proximal obstruction, but cornual spasm, mucus or technical factors can mimic this.

items: Pattern 4: Hydrosalpinx or distal tubal disease

blocks.text: Dilated, tortuous tube.
Absent or restricted free spill, sometimes with retained contrast.
Interpretation: Suggestive of distal tubal obstruction and hydrosalpinx.
These images illustrate typical patterns; actual interpretation should be based on the complete study and formal radiology report.

Distal obstruction, impaired passage or technical limitation
True occlusion or transient spasm/technical artefact

blocks.text: A proximal block on HSG does not always mean permanent tubal occlusion. Tubal spasm, mucus or catheter-related technical issues can produce a false-positive result.
Depending on the clinical context, confirmation may involve repeat imaging, selective salpingography with possible cannulation, or another appropriate investigation.

content_groups.group_title: HyCoSy: how to explain and perform it

blocks.text: HyCoSy assesses the passage of contrast through the tubes using ultrasound rather than X-ray.
Confirm identity, consent and absence of pregnancy or active infection.
Explain the procedure and offer appropriate analgesia.
Position the patient, usually in lithotomy.
Insert a speculum and introduce a suitable transcervical catheter.
Use transvaginal ultrasound to assess the uterus and adnexa.
Introduce the contrast agent or suitable fluid according to the local protocol.
Observe contrast passage through the tubes and assess for evidence of spill.
Remove the catheter, assess the patient and arrange follow-up.
No ionising radiation.
May be combined with pelvic ultrasound assessment.
Can assess the uterus and ovaries in the same visit.
Often well tolerated in an outpatient setting.
Operator-dependent.
Tubes may be difficult to visualise.
Results can be inconclusive.
It may not reliably identify peritubal adhesions or all forms of pelvic pathology.
Exam point: HyCoSy is a reasonable alternative to HSG where suitable expertise and equipment are available.
This is a surgical procedure, not a routine first-line investigation for every woman with infertility.
Consider it when there is a clinical reason to inspect the pelvis directly, such as:
Suspected endometriosis.
Significant pelvic pain or suspected adhesions.
Previous pelvic infection or surgery with concern for tubal damage.
Abnormal or inconclusive non-surgical tubal assessment when the result would alter management.
Another indication for operative pelvic assessment.
Obtain informed consent for laparoscopy, dye testing and any agreed additional procedures.
Administer general anaesthesia.
Establish laparoscopic access using the appropriate surgical technique.
Inspect the uterus, ovaries, tubes and pelvis.
Introduce dye through the cervix.
Observe the fimbrial ends of the tubes for dye spill.
Identify adhesions, endometriosis, hydrosalpinx or other pathology.
Perform additional surgery only when indicated, consented to and clinically appropriate.
Direct visualisation of pelvic anatomy.
Can identify endometriosis and adhesions that HSG may miss.
May allow treatment during the same operation.
Anaesthetic complications.
Bleeding, infection and postoperative pain.
Injury to bowel, bladder, blood vessels or other organs.
Risks associated with additional operative procedures.
Do not recommend laparoscopy simply because it is more invasive. The likely benefit must justify the surgical risks and costs.

blocks.text: Patients should seek urgent medical review if they develop severe or worsening abdominal pain, fever, heavy bleeding, fainting or symptoms of a serious allergic reaction after the procedure.
Tubal findings must be interpreted alongside age, ovarian reserve, ovulation, semen analysis, duration of infertility and the patient's reproductive goals.

items: Abnormal or suspicious tubal patency test
Review image quality, clinical history and other infertility results

blocks.text: Assess the other tube and all other fertility factors. Individualise expectant management or treatment.
Confirm clinically important obstruction and discuss fertility-specialist referral and assisted conception.
Consider repeat assessment or selective tubal cannulation in suitable cases.
Discuss fertility-specialist management; treatment before IVF may improve outcomes in appropriate patients.
Management depends on whether the other tube is normal, the patient's age, duration of infertility and other fertility factors.
Options may include expectant management in selected cases, treatment of associated conditions, or assisted reproduction if conception does not occur or other factors are present.
First consider whether the result may be false-positive.
If obstruction is confirmed, options in selected patients include:
Selective salpingography and tubal cannulation.
Assisted reproductive technology, particularly IVF.
Individualised counselling regarding the chance of success, risks and costs.

content_groups.group_title: C. Distal tubal disease and hydrosalpinx

blocks.text: Hydrosalpinx can reduce IVF implantation and pregnancy outcomes. Depending on anatomy and fertility goals, a specialist may recommend salpingectomy or proximal tubal occlusion before IVF.
Tubal reconstructive surgery may be suitable for selected patients, but success depends on the severity and location of damage and the patient's overall fertility profile.
A normal test does not complete the infertility evaluation. Assess other factors, including ovulation, ovarian reserve when indicated, uterine pathology, intercourse timing and semen analysis.
Prevention of further tubal damage includes:
Prompt diagnosis and treatment of sexually transmitted infections.
Appropriate partner evaluation and treatment when indicated.
Safer-sex counselling.
Early assessment of pelvic pain, fever or abnormal discharge suggestive of PID.
Q1. What is the first-line investigation for tubal patency?

HSG or HyCoSy is commonly used as a first-line investigation in women without a strong history or symptoms suggesting significant pelvic pathology. The choice depends on availability, expertise, contraindications and patient preference.
Q2. When should HSG be performed?
Usually after menstruation has ended and before ovulation, after pregnancy has been excluded and active pelvic infection has been ruled out.
Q3. What does free peritoneal spill mean?
Contrast has passed through the fallopian tube and is seen escaping from its fimbrial end into the peritoneal cavity. This supports anatomical tubal patency.
Q4. Does a patent tube guarantee fertility?
No. It does not establish normal fimbrial pickup, ciliary function, tubal motility or all aspects of tubal function.
Q5. Why can HSG falsely diagnose proximal obstruction?
Transient tubal spasm, mucus, inadequate contrast pressure or technical factors may prevent visible filling.
Q6. What is the difference between HSG and laparoscopy with chromopertubation?
HSG is a radiographic test that outlines the uterine cavity and tubes. Laparoscopy allows direct inspection of pelvic structures and dye spill, and may reveal adhesions or endometriosis.
Q7. Why is laparoscopy not routine for every infertile woman?
It is invasive and carries anaesthetic and surgical risks. Non-surgical testing is usually sufficient initially when there is no clinical suspicion of significant pelvic pathology.
Q8. What is hydrosalpinx?
A distended fallopian tube containing fluid, commonly due to distal tubal obstruction and damage. It may impair fertility and reduce IVF success.
Q9. How would you manage bilateral tubal occlusion?

Review the study and consider confirmation if false-positive proximal obstruction is possible. Assess the patient's age, ovarian reserve, semen analysis and reproductive goals, then discuss suitable options, including tubal cannulation in selected proximal disease or IVF for significant bilateral damage.
Q10. What complications must you counsel about before HSG?
Pain, cramping, spotting, vasovagal symptoms, infection and contrast reaction. Uterine injury is uncommon but possible.
Q11. Is prophylactic antibiotic treatment necessary for everyone undergoing HSG?

Not necessarily. Practice depends on risk factors and local protocol. Patients with active infection require assessment and treatment before the procedure; selected patients with previous PID or hydrosalpinx may need specific prophylactic measures.
Q12. What would you do if a patient develops severe pain and fever after HSG?
Arrange urgent clinical assessment for pelvic infection or another complication, assess vital signs and haemodynamic stability, and initiate appropriate investigations and treatment.
Performing or recommending HSG without excluding pregnancy.
Overlooking active pelvic infection.
Assuming that bilateral proximal non-filling proves permanent obstruction.
Describing tubal patency as proof of normal fertility.
Recommending laparoscopy as the first investigation for every patient.
Ignoring the semen analysis and ovulatory assessment when interpreting abnormal tubal findings.
Failing to explain discomfort, complications and follow-up.
Treating the image without considering the patient's clinical history.
P — Pregnancy excluded.
I — Infection assessed.
C — Contrast history and relevant contraindications reviewed.
T — Timing appropriate, generally before ovulation.
F — Filling of the uterine cavity and tubes.
S — Site of suspected obstruction.
C — Contrast spill into the peritoneal cavity.
B — Both partners assessed.
O — Other fertility factors considered.
